title: Readers’ Rides: Sean’s Vertebra Bikes Full Suspension
content:
Sometimes a bike lands in your lap that presents a great mystery. Sean Higgins came across a unique vintage mountain bike in a back alley, and it led him on a journey into Colorado framebuilding history…

One evening my partner Kari came home from a walk in our neighborhood in Fort Collins, CO, and mentioned seeing what appeared to be an abandoned bike a few blocks from our place, leaning up against a fence in an alley. I was definitely curious, but I didn’t give it much more thought until I drove by a few days later and noticed the bike still there propped up against the fence. It didn’t look like any bike or brand that I recognized – just a slightly odd-looking white mountain bike. Debating if I should get involved, I thought that if the bike stuck around a little while longer I would grab it and try to find it’s owner.

We finally walked over to properly investigate a day or two later. Approaching the bike, I first I thought it could be a Richard Cunningham-designed Nishiki Alien because it appeared to have elevated chain-stays and a non-traditional frame design. But as we got closer, I started to realize that it wasn’t a Nishiki, or anything like it, but something a bit wilder. The tires were flat and badly dry-rotten, but from a quick glance it had pretty nice ‘80s/‘90s XT level components, Specialized flag cranks and a very custom full-suspension frame…I decided in this moment that the bike had been abandoned long enough, so I hoisted it on one shoulder and we walked back to our place.

Once home and in my garage, I finally got a good look at what I was dealing with and the mystery only deepened. I know a fair bit about ‘80s/‘90s mountain bikes, but I’d never seen a bike like this before. All the components looked original from the period, and I surmised that this thing hadn’t been ridden in many years. The bike had no markings that I could decipher, no serial number or makers mark. I figured out that the fork was an Action Tec from the peeling decals on the legs, similar in design to, but on the market before the Cannondale HeadShok, but that wasn’t much help.

I couldn’t quite figure out why this bike looked so strange to me aside from the obviously unique full-suspension frame. The frame design has no regular pivot, instead it has a flexible piece of steel on which the swing arm rotates. Then I realized, oh, it has 24-inch wheels! That explains the unfamiliar proportions. With smaller wheels, the frame has room for the suspension components to be inline above the wheels.

With all the buzz surrounding 32 inch wheels these days, what about the fun of 24? I started to think that if I can figure out who made this bike, I can figure out to whom it belongs. It was clearly made by someone who knows a thing or two about engineering and is experienced at making frames. Looking at the complex curves of the swingarm it’s obvious this wasn’t just a one-oﬀ bike build, but made by someone with experience.

With no spare 24-inch tubes lying around, I pumped some air in the old cracked tires and headed over to my local bike shop, Brave New Wheel, luckily only a few blocks away. I was hoping the guys there would recognize the bike, that maybe it had been in the shop before. I showed the bike to one of Brave’s owners, Johnny Daggett, but he unfortunately didn’t recognize it. Everyone in the shop that day wanted to check out the curious bike and take it for a spin around the block. They all agreed that it was a super fun bike, perfect for hopping oﬀ a curb or hitting some urban trails.

Johnny oﬀered to ask around to see if anyone knew anything about the bike and I gave him my number in case he found a lead. He snapped a few pictures and I took the bike back home. Another dead end, but I was happy to hang on to this mystery bike for a while longer.

A few days later, the mystery – of who built the bike, at least – was solved. I received a call from an unknown number, which turned out to be the bike’s maker. Johnny at Brave had sent pictures over to a local bike collector, Jeﬀ Nye, who recognized the bike and got in touch with the bike’s builder, Jon Lebsack. I called the number back, and Jon and I chatted for a while about how I ended up with the bike, then made a plan to meet for lunch so he could check out his lost machine.

Jon built bikes in Fort Collins in the ’80s and early ‘90s, with this particular bike being one of his last, a prototype from 1992. His company was called Vertebra Bikes (“We provide the bones-you provide the meat!”) which focused on mountain bikes. One of his bikes – ridden by sponsored rider Wade Wilderman out of Fraser, CO – placed 17th in the first Mountain Bike World Championship in 1990.

Jon also built race-winning road bikes, a handful of recumbents, a very early fat bike (two tires sewn together to make one), a two-wheel drive mountain bike and some machines for human powered speed records. Jon is a tinkerer and has the mind of an engineer and had skills with a torch.

Some time ago Jon gave the bike away and then lost track of it over the intervening years. In lieu of a better solution, Jon told me that I should just keep the bike, which I was more than happy to do. In the intervening months, I’ve done the minimum to make it trail- worthy. I put on some new 24-inch tires and tubes, swapped out the saddle, changed the brake pads and added a new Simworks handlebar to help make the ‘90s MTB riding position more comfortable. I’ve left everything else as is, including the brazed, unpainted stem riser.

Jon has been super generous with his time and my questions about his bike-building career. He recently found the original stem that he made for the bike in his parts stash which he gifted to me and I added to the bike. At some point I will need to rebuild the Action Tec fork and AMP shock but I’m not exactly sure where I’d start so hopefully Jon will be willing to help. I’m guessing there isn’t a good YouTube tutorial out there.

I am really enjoying bumping around town on the bike and people are always curious what it is. It rides great and puts a smile on my face every time I throw a leg over it. The bike rides a bit like a mini-velo and because of the small wheels it really does love to wheelie! These days Jon is retired which allows him to ride as much as possible on his road bikes or on his ‘90s mountain bikes converted into gravel rigs. He puts in a ton of miles. He recently brought back into service a very sweet, bright yellow, original Vertebra frame from 1989 that’s been hanging in his garage for many years. It’s been great getting to know Jon and his bikes, a nice outcome of rescuing an abandoned bike.

I am no closer to finding out how the bike ended up ditched in the alley, but in the meantime I’m really happy to be its steward. It goes without saying that I’d still like to get it back to whomever lost it, so if anyone sees this and recognizes who owned it last, please let me know. Until then I’ll keep enjoying my Vertebra prototype!

Build Spec:

  • Custom hand-built frame, stem and swingarm, Vertebra Bikes prototype
  • Action-Tec Pro Shock front fork, 44mm (I think)
  • AMP research rear coil shock, unsure of the travel
  • Shimano Deore XT derailleur
  • Shimano Deore XT thumb shifters, 3×6
  • Specialized flag crankset
  • Sun Chinook 24 inch rims laced to Suntour front hub/Shimano 105 rear
  • Simworks Fun 3 Bar in CrMo
